promptText: What defines a functional interface in Java, and what commonly-misunderstood exception exists?
options: It must have exactly one abstract method (SAM), but it may also declare any number of default and static methods, which don't count against that rule since they already have bodies
It must have exactly one method total, with no default or static methods permitted at all
It cannot redeclare any public method already defined on Object, such as equals() or toString()
The @FunctionalInterface annotation is mandatory; without it, the interface cannot be used as a lambda target
explanation: The single abstract method gives the compiler a target a lambda can implement; default/static methods already carry an implementation so they're exempt, a functional interface MAY redeclare Object's public methods without breaking the rule, and @FunctionalInterface is only an optional safety net, not a requirement for lambda compatibility.

promptText: Why must a local variable captured inside a lambda be final or effectively final (never reassigned after initialization)?
options: The lambda may outlive the method's stack frame (e.g. run later on another thread), so Java captures the variable's value at that point in time rather than a live reference to the local variable itself
Java lambdas execute in a separate memory space that cannot access the enclosing method's stack at all
Only effectively final variables can be autoboxed into the functional interface's parameter type
This restriction only applies to lambdas that are passed to a Thread constructor, not general lambdas
explanation: Since the lambda might execute long after the enclosing method has returned, Java captures a snapshot of the variable's value rather than tying it to the method's stack frame; allowing reassignment after capture would create ambiguous semantics about which value the lambda should see, so the compiler forbids it (instance/static fields are unaffected since they don't live on the stack).

promptText: A Collection can be iterated many times, but a Stream can only be consumed once. Why is this the case?
options: A stream is a lazy, one-shot pipeline of computation rather than a stored data structure; once a terminal operation closes it, reusing the same stream instance throws IllegalStateException
Streams physically delete their source collection's elements as they are processed
Collections are always lazy while Streams are always eager, which is the reverse of the actual behavior
A Stream can be reused as many times as needed, identical to a Collection, once you call stream() a second time on the same instance
explanation: A Collection materializes and stores its elements for repeated access, while a Stream is a declarative pipeline that pulls elements through only as a terminal operation demands them; that one-shot design is what enables laziness and short-circuiting, but it also means the same stream object cannot be iterated twice -- you must obtain a fresh stream from the source.

promptText: A method changes its return type from `User` (nullable) to `Optional<User>`. What concretely improves as a result?
options: The possibility of absence becomes part of the compile-time contract, nudging the caller to explicitly handle the empty case (e.g. via orElseThrow) instead of risking a forgotten null check and a runtime NullPointerException
The method itself becomes faster because Optional avoids a heap allocation for the returned value
Optional guarantees the method can never throw an exception during its computation
Callers no longer need to handle the empty case at all, since Optional resolves it automatically
explanation: Optional's value is purely at the type-system level: it documents that 'no result' is a legitimate outcome and provides a fluent API (map/filter/orElseThrow) to handle it declaratively, but it adds a wrapper allocation rather than removing one, does not prevent exceptions, and still requires the caller to explicitly decide what happens on empty.

promptText: Why does replacing a hand-written POJO with a Java `record` reduce a common class of real bugs, beyond just saving lines of code?
options: The compiler generates equals(), hashCode(), and toString() consistently from every declared component in one place, eliminating the classic mistake of adding a new field but forgetting to update equals() to include it
Records automatically add method-level synchronization to every generated accessor for thread safety
Records support multiple inheritance of state from more than one parent class, unlike POJOs
Records are mutable by default, which prevents a whole class of concurrency bugs POJOs suffer from
explanation: A hand-written equals()/hashCode() must be manually kept in sync with the class's fields, and forgetting to include a newly-added field is a very common, hard-to-spot bug; records generate these methods directly from the declared components, so they can never drift out of sync -- records are also implicitly final and immutable, the opposite of the last two distractors.

promptText: What is the core idea behind Java 21 virtual threads, and what is the most common misconception about them?
options: They are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM and multiplexed onto a small pool of OS carrier threads, enabling millions of concurrent tasks; the common misconception is that they make an individual computation run faster, when really they only increase how many blocked tasks can be held cheaply
They are a new type of thread that executes CPU-bound computations faster than platform threads by using SIMD instructions
They eliminate the need for any locking or synchronization since each virtual thread has fully isolated memory
They replace the common ForkJoinPool used by parallel streams for CPU-bound work
explanation: Virtual threads don't speed up any single task's computation; the win is that a blocked virtual thread detaches from its carrier thread, letting another virtual thread run, so a server can support vastly more concurrent I/O-bound tasks -- they still share heap memory like any thread and are not a replacement for parallel-stream CPU parallelism.

promptText: What is the key difference between the Stream operations map() and flatMap(), and what result type mistake does a candidate typically make by reaching for map() out of habit?
options: map() is a strict one-to-one transformation; flatMap() maps each element to its own stream and flattens all resulting streams into one -- using map() on a stream of lists produces an awkward Stream<List<T>> instead of a flat Stream<T>
map() can both increase and decrease the number of elements in the stream, while flatMap() always preserves the original count
flatMap() only operates on primitive int/long/double streams, never on object streams
map() and flatMap() are fully interchangeable in every scenario, differing only in performance
explanation: Applying map() to a stream of lists yields a stream of lists (Stream<List<String>>) because map() emits exactly one output per input; flatMap() instead maps each element to a stream and merges all of those streams into one flat sequence, which is the tool needed whenever you want to collapse nested structures rather than just transform elements.

promptText: Why is `sorted()` called a 'stateful' intermediate operation, and what does that cost you compared to `filter()` or `map()`?
options: sorted() must buffer every element of the stream before it can emit even the first sorted element, which defeats laziness and blocks any short-circuiting operation placed after it until the whole stream has been consumed
sorted() mutates the original source collection in place, unlike filter() or map()
sorted() can only be used as the very last operation in a pipeline, never followed by any other intermediate operation
sorted() always throws an exception unless every element implements Comparable, even when a Comparator is supplied
explanation: Unlike filter/map, which process one element at a time and can pass it straight through the pipeline, sorted() inherently needs to see every element before it can determine what comes first, so it forces full buffering and prevents genuine short-circuiting through that point in the pipeline -- a real performance consideration on large datasets.

promptText: Why is `optional.orElse(repository.findDefault())` a subtle production bug, whereas `optional.orElseGet(() -> repository.findDefault())` is not?
options: orElse()'s argument is evaluated eagerly every time the line executes, so it hits the database even when the Optional already holds a value; orElseGet()'s Supplier is invoked only when the Optional is actually empty
orElse() and orElseGet() behave identically at runtime; the difference is purely stylistic with no performance implication
orElseGet() cannot accept any expression that throws a checked exception, while orElse() can
orElse() caches the result of its argument across all future calls on the same Optional instance
explanation: Because Java evaluates method arguments before the call happens, orElse(expensiveCall()) always executes expensiveCall(), discarding the result if the Optional is present; orElseGet() defers that work into a Supplier invoked only on the empty path, which matters enormously when the default value is expensive or has side effects like a database call.

promptText: What happens when two elements in a stream map to the same key inside `Collectors.toMap(keyMapper, valueMapper)`, and how do you fix it?
options: It throws IllegalStateException because the two-argument overload has no way to resolve the collision; supplying a third merge-function argument tells the collector how to combine the colliding values
The second value silently overwrites the first with no error or warning
The collector automatically wraps colliding values into a List, converting the map into a Map<K, List<V>>
toMap() ignores duplicate keys and keeps only the first occurrence, discarding the rest silently
explanation: The two-argument toMap() has no strategy for a key collision and fails fast with IllegalStateException specifically to avoid silently dropping data; the three-argument overload adds a BinaryOperator merge function so you explicitly decide how to combine two values that land on the same key.

promptText: Why can using a parallel stream for a blocking database call inside a web server degrade performance for completely unrelated requests?
options: By default, parallel streams run on the JVM-wide shared common ForkJoinPool; blocking those pool threads on I/O starves every other parallel stream in the process, not just the one performing the blocking call
Parallel streams require a dedicated database connection per CPU core, exhausting the connection pool immediately
Parallel streams disable the JIT compiler for the duration of the stream operation, slowing all other code globally
Each element processed in parallel opens a brand-new database transaction that is never closed
explanation: The common ForkJoinPool is shared across the entire JVM, so any code -- including unrelated library internals -- that also relies on parallel streams or ForkJoinTask can be starved if your blocking I/O ties up its limited worker threads; this is why blocking or database work should use a dedicated Executor (e.g. via CompletableFuture) rather than a default parallel stream.

promptText: You need to first fetch a user, then use that user's id to asynchronously fetch their orders. Why is thenCompose() the correct choice here instead of thenApply()?
options: The order-fetching function itself returns a CompletableFuture, so thenApply() would produce an awkward nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Orders>>; thenCompose() flattens that into a single CompletableFuture<Orders>, mirroring Stream.flatMap()
thenCompose() runs synchronously on the calling thread while thenApply() always spawns a new thread
thenApply() can only be used once per CompletableFuture chain, while thenCompose() can be chained indefinitely
thenCompose() is required whenever the previous stage completed exceptionally, while thenApply() is only for successful completions
explanation: thenApply() expects a plain value-returning Function, so feeding it a function that itself returns a CompletableFuture creates a nested future you'd have to unwrap manually; thenCompose() is designed exactly for this dependent-async-operation case, flattening the result the same way flatMap() flattens nested streams.

promptText: An aggregator fetches a user, their orders, and their payments from three independent services. Compared to calling them sequentially, why does launching each with supplyAsync and merging with allOf/thenCombine reduce total latency to roughly the slowest call rather than the sum of all three -- and what must be true of the three calls for this benefit to hold?
options: Because the three calls have no dependency on each other, they can execute concurrently on separate threads (ideally a dedicated Executor, not just the common pool); if one call actually depended on another's result, this concurrent-launch benefit would disappear and thenCompose-style chaining would be required instead
The benefit holds unconditionally, even if each call depends on the previous call's result, because CompletableFuture reorders dependent calls automatically
Total latency is reduced only because CompletableFuture caches identical calls across requests, not because of concurrency
This pattern works only when all three calls target the exact same downstream service
explanation: Concurrent execution only shrinks total latency to roughly max(call1, call2, call3) when the calls are truly independent of one another; if fetching orders required the user's id from the first call, you would need thenCompose to express that dependency, and the calls could no longer all start at the same time, changing the latency math back toward sequential.

promptText: A sealed interface `Shape` permits only `Circle` and `Square`. A switch expression over a `Shape` handles both cases with no default branch and compiles successfully. What happens if a developer later adds a new permitted subtype `Triangle` but forgets to update the switch?
options: The switch is no longer exhaustive, so the code fails to compile until the new Triangle case is added -- this compiler-enforced exhaustiveness is the main reason sealed classes pair so well with pattern-matching switches
The switch silently falls through to whichever case is listed last, with no compiler warning
Triangle is automatically treated as equivalent to Circle since both were declared in the same permits list originally
Sealed classes only affect inheritance, not switch statements, so the switch continues to compile and simply never matches Triangle at runtime
explanation: Because the compiler knows the complete, closed set of a sealed type's permitted subtypes, it can verify a switch handles every one of them; adding a new permitted subtype without updating every exhaustive switch over that type immediately breaks the build, which is precisely the safety net sealed types are designed to provide over an ordinary open class hierarchy.

promptText: On a sequential stream, findFirst() and findAny() behave identically. Why does the distinction only start to matter -- and specifically favor findAny() -- once the stream is made parallel?
options: findFirst() must still honor encounter order even under parallel execution, requiring extra cross-thread coordination to determine which result is truly "first"; findAny() has no such ordering obligation and can return as soon as any thread finds a match, avoiding that coordination cost
findAny() is not supported at all on parallel streams and silently falls back to sequential execution
findFirst() cannot be combined with a preceding filter() in a parallel pipeline
findAny() always returns a different result than findFirst() would, even on the exact same data
explanation: Both return an Optional and both short-circuit, but findFirst()'s contract to always return the first element in encounter order forces the parallel implementation to coordinate across threads to confirm ordering, while findAny() is free to return whichever match a thread happens to find first -- so when you genuinely don't care which match you get, findAny() avoids paying for a guarantee you don't need.
